rewriteLast.title: Chapter 8 · A Wedding in the Old Garden
rewriteLast.artPrompt: a garden wedding beneath a flowering cherry tree at a mossy old lodge, a small white-haired bride in soft white and a tall brown-eyed gentleman holding hands, a curly-haired boy scattering rose petals, a little maid in a starched apron dabbing happy tears, golden summer morning light, storybook illustration

blocks.text: At last the great day came. Miss Lavender Lewis was to be married in the old garden at Echo Lodge. The roses, everyone said, had been waiting years for this. Nobody in Avonlea had talked of anything else all week. Paul Irving walked up the mossy path with his heart drumming. The bride was his dearest friend. The groom was his own father. He had begged the honor of carrying the rings, and his pockets had been checked nine times that morning.
The vows beneath the flowering cherry, while the echo applauds from the garden wall.

Little Charlotta the Fourth, the lodge maid, cried into her starched apron and smiled at the same time. Anne stood close by and held Paul's hand at the important moments. Under the flowering cherry, the small white-haired bride and the tall brown-eyed gentleman promised each other the years to come. Nobody had ever seen the old garden look so glad. When the little company clapped, the echo clapped back, and Miss Lavender laughed and cried at once.
Talk together: A foolish quarrel kept the bride and groom apart for many years. What helps people say sorry after a long, long time?

Paul thought it the finest thing in the history of the world, and nobody present cared to argue. After the vows he shyly gave the bride white phlox from his grandmother's garden. She kissed him before everybody, and he beamed as if he had been made a knight. Charlotta the Fourth declared she would remember it all her life, and she did. The echo said yes, yes, to every promise. Anne thought the echo had waited long enough for somebody to answer back.

All afternoon the old garden rang with talk and laughter, and cake was cut under the wisteria. When Anne walked home through the gold September light, Paul waved from the gate until she was out of sight. Behind her the cherry dropped its petals like soft white rain, and the echo kept on blessing everybody it could hear.

chapters.title: Chapter 9 · Davy in Search of a Fairy
chapters.artPrompt: a small gap-toothed boy in a nightshirt asleep on a stool beside an old garden well in silver moonlight, fir trees and pale flowers around him, a lantern glowing far off at a farmhouse window, deep blue night, storybook illustration

blocks.text: Anne told the twins fairy stories on rainy evenings, and Davy listened with his mouth open. He asked questions all day long — about stars, about hens, about everything. Dora, who was tidy and good, kept her doubts to herself. One night he asked where fairies lived. 'In gardens,' said Anne, 'if you look for them properly.' She meant it for a joke, and forgot it by breakfast. Davy did not forget it at all.
Davy keeps faithful watch by the old well in the silver moonlight.

That night, when the house was asleep, Davy crept out of bed. He carried a stool to the old well in the garden, set it down, and sat waiting. The garden was silver and shadow. The moon looked over the fir trees like a round white fairy herself. Once an owl hooted, and Davy gripped the stool with both hands. He watched and watched until his eyes grew heavy, and then he fell fast asleep, still on duty.
New word: on duty — keeping watch at a job, the way a soldier or a lighthouse keeper does. Talk together: Anne meant her fairy remark as fun. Why did Davy take it seriously?

Marilla found the empty bed and gave a cry that woke the household. Mrs. Rachel Lynde seized a lantern, and they searched the garden and the orchard, calling softly. Anne's heart had been thumping with fright the whole time. At last the lantern light fell on Davy, sound asleep among the shadows, with a little cold already settling in his nose. He was carried back to bed half awake, protesting that he had nearly seen one.

He was dosed with Mrs. Lynde's bitterest medicine, which he said was worse than any fairy. 'But did you see one?' Anne asked him next morning. 'No, I fell asleep,' Davy owned. 'But I'm going to try again when I'm better.' Anne gave up explaining. A boy who would sit all night by a well for the sake of a fairy, she decided, was a kindred spirit in the making.

chapters.title: Chapter 10 · A Jonah Day
chapters.artPrompt: a young teacher with red braids standing wearily at the blackboard of a one-room schoolhouse while rain streams down the tall windows, children at wooden desks watching her sideways, a jar of wild roses on the desk, grey rainy daylight, storybook illustration

blocks.text: Some days begin badly and then get worse, and this was one. Anne overslept, and the porridge had lumps in it. Davy came to school with a loose tooth and a plan for showing it to everybody. At school the ink bottle upset across the cleanest desk. The little ones quarreled over nothing, the big ones whispered riddles, and the spelling lesson went from bad to dreadful.
A long, grey day at the Avonlea school, with one very discouraged teacher.

Worst of all, Anne lost her temper. She said sharp things she did not mean, and kept the whole school in when the sun was calling. Even Paul's fairy tales could not brighten the morning. All day a small voice inside kept whispering, You can do better than this, Anne Shirley. But the day rolled downhill like a cart without brakes, and she could not stop it.
New word: Jonah day — a day when everything goes wrong, named for the old sea story of Jonah. Everyone has such days. What matters is what you do the next morning.

The rain tapped on the window as if apologizing. She walked home through a drizzle, feeling like a failure in a gingham dress. Marilla saw her face and asked no questions, which was sometimes the kindest thing. Mrs. Rachel Lynde saw it too, and arrived with a plate of doughnuts and her own kind of comfort. Nobody, said Mrs. Lynde, ever yet made a day better by sitting up all night feeling bad about it.

Next morning Anne was at the schoolhouse before the bell, with wild roses in a jar and a fresh start in her heart. The roses, she found, made the whole room smell like a new beginning. She smiled at every scholar as the door banged open and shut. By noon the school hummed like a beehive. That night she wrote in her diary that she had been a Jonah on Tuesday, and meant to be the sun on Wednesday.

chapters.title: Chapter 11 · Mr. Harrison's Wife
chapters.artPrompt: a trim little woman in a grey dress laughing at a fat elderly gentleman in a vest on a farm-gate lane, a green parrot screaming from a porch post between them, hollyhocks and a tidy farmhouse behind, bright afternoon light, storybook illustration

blocks.text: Mr. Harrison had always said he was a widower, briskly, and nobody had thought to doubt him. Then one afternoon a trim little woman in a grey dress stopped at Green Gables and asked the way to Mr. Harrison's. She said she was his wife. She said it quite calmly, as if reporting the price of eggs. Marilla was shelling peas on the step and dropped a whole pod.
A polite stranger at the Green Gables gate, carrying surprising news.

Anne guided her down the lane, so full of questions that she could hardly speak them. It seemed that a foolish quarrel, years and years ago, had parted him from the girl he married. There had been no letters, no parting, only silence on both sides. He had gone off to be a farmer and a bachelor, and she had waited for him to come to his senses. Now she had decided she had waited long enough.
Talk together: Mr. Harrison let his neighbors believe a wrong thing rather than explain an old sorrow. Why is the truth, even an awkward truth, usually the better plan?

At the gate of the next farm, the meeting began badly. Mr. Harrison stood there like a man caught stealing jam. Ginger, his parrot, broke the silence with language no parrot should know. The little lady looked at the bird, then at her husband, and began to laugh. Mrs. Harrison had not laughed so much in twenty years.

She was still laughing when she held out her hand. Mr. Harrison mopped his forehead, muttered that the bird would be docked a week's crackers, and took the hand. Before the week was out, Avonlea knew that Mrs. Harrison had come to stay. Anne wrote in her diary that night. A stubborn man, a swearing parrot, and twenty years of silence, she decided, were no match for a determined woman. Ginger, for his part, was granted crackers all the same.

chapters.title: Chapter 12 · The Story Club Is Formed
chapters.artPrompt: four girls seated in a circle in a cozy parlor with curtains drawn, one girl with red braids reading from a paper manuscript while the others giggle and lean in, a kettle steaming on the stove, warm lamplight, storybook illustration

blocks.text: One golden evening, walking home from school, Anne had one of her splendid ideas. 'Let us have a Story Club,' she cried. 'We shall each write stories and read them aloud, like famous authors.' Diana Barry clapped her hands. Jane Andrews said it would be useful. Ruby Gillis said it would be romantic. It was settled before they reached the lane's end. Her head was so full of heroes that she nearly walked past Green Gables by mistake.
The founding meeting of the Story Club, with the manuscript held high.

They met once a week at Diana's, very solemnly, with the door shut. Each member read a story aloud, and the others made remarks. The remarks were supposed to be serious. Mostly they were giggles, for Ruby's heroes fainted too often, and Jane's heroines did nothing but keep house. Anne's stories were full of storms, vows, and beautiful sad ladies, and the club agreed they were nearly as good as printed books.
Talk together: If you had a Story Club, what kind of story would you write first — a storm, a secret, or a journey?

Anne wrote the club's masterpiece, a thrilling tale called Averil's Atonement, which she read in her best reading voice. Averil, the heroine, suffered magnificently for eleven pages. The club sat spellbound, and even the kettle seemed to listen. Diana declared it was as good as anything in a real magazine. That was when the dangerous idea came to Anne.

'What if,' said Anne slowly, 'a real magazine printed it?' The club gasped. Authors, surely, were people in far cities with ink on their fingers. She copied the story out fair that very night, in her roundest handwriting. She read it over twice, trembled at her own boldness, and mailed it away. The story flew off to the city like a pigeon with a secret. Then she told no one, and waited, and jumped every time the mail came.

chapters.title: Chapter 13 · Averil's Atonement
chapters.artPrompt: a young woman with red braids at a garden table staring in comic dismay at a small magazine stuffed with medicine advertisements, her best friend laughing beside her, an envelope and a bank check on the table, bright summer noon, storybook illustration

blocks.text: The answer came in a long white envelope with a printed stamp. Anne carried it unopened to the garden, because her hands were shaking too much for the kitchen. Inside was a letter: her story had been accepted. Enclosed was a check for ten whole dollars. Ten dollars, for a story with her own name signed at the bottom of it. She read it four times to be sure the numbers did not change.
Ten shining dollars' worth of literary fame, in one thin envelope.

She told Diana first, then the club, then Green Gables, then Avonlea. Mrs. Rachel Lynde sniffed that writing stories never yet buttered bread, but she read Averil's Atonement twice all the same. Even Marilla's lips twitched, though she called it silliness. Davy asked if he might have a dollar, and was told firmly no. Anne walked on air for a week and began her next masterpiece in her head.
New word: atonement — making up for a wrong thing that was done. Anne's heroine spent eleven pages doing it. Talk together: which is harder, saying sorry or waiting to be forgiven?

Then the magazine itself arrived, and Anne sat down to behold herself in print. The magazine was small and discouraging. Even the paper smelled like a drugstore. It was crammed from cover to cover with advertisements for patent medicines. Cure-all syrups and floating pills crowded every page. Averil's Atonement lay squeezed between advertisements for hair dye and cough syrup.

For one dreadful minute Anne wanted to dig a hole and get into it. Then Diana came over, read one page, and laughed until she had to sit on the floor. It was impossible to be tragic with Diana laughing, so Anne laughed too, until her sides ached. She kept the check, and the little magazine too. Together they proved she was a published author — and still had a great deal to learn. Years afterward she could not tell the tale without laughing at herself first.

chapters.title: Chapter 14 · Paul Shines Forth
chapters.artPrompt: a curly-haired boy and a young woman with red braids looking up in wonder at an enormous golden-tipped pine tree at the edge of a field, the boy gesturing proudly, sunset light flooding through dark boughs, storybook illustration

blocks.text: Paul Irving was the best scholar in the school and the worst speller in the county. His spelling, to be fair, had improved by exactly one mistake a month. On composition day he handed in a page with the word 'which' spelled four different ways. But his composition was about the great bright pine that grew behind his grandmother's field, and nobody who read it laughed at anything.
Paul reads his essay about the big bright pine while the class listens.

He had written how the pine stood taller than the orchard, straight as a hero in a story. How he told it his secrets after school, and how it talked back in a language of whispers. How, on the worst day of his life, he had leaned against it and felt less alone. Then Anne read it aloud to the school. The room went completely quiet, in the way that is better than clapping.
Talk together: Paul talks to a tree and feels heard. Do you have a place — or a tree, or a corner — where it is easier to think? What makes a place like that?

When it ended, the big scholars stamped their feet, and Anthony Pye led the cheering, which surprised everyone most of all. Paul went very red and looked unbearably pleased, exactly as a boy should. Davy, in the front row, decided he would write an essay too, about a hen. Anne kept his essay folded in her desk drawer all term. Now that his father had married Miss Lavender, Paul had two gardens to love him. Somebody in each was always glad to see him.

After school Paul begged her to come and see the tree itself. They went through the golden field, and there it stood against the sunset, vast and gold-tipped and very great. Paul introduced Anne to it formally, as one friend to another, and stood listening to the whisper. 'You see?' he said. 'It remembers everything.' Anne, looking up through the dark boughs, quite believed him.
